items.stem: Which model emphasises several separate centres of activity in a city?
items.answer: The multiple nuclei model
items.markingKey: The multiple nuclei model. Harris and Ullman (1945) noted specialised nuclei such as industrial areas and suburban centres.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the sector model and the concentric zone model.
items.answer: The concentric model arranges land uses in rings around the CBD; the sector model arranges them in wedges along transport routes from the centre.
items.markingKey: The concentric model arranges land uses in rings around the CBD; the sector model arranges them in wedges along transport routes from the centre. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why cities develop distinct sectors of land use.
items.answer: Transport routes, relief, rivers and early high-status areas attract similar uses, which then expand outward along routes (Hoyt), e.g. industrial corridors along railways.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Transport routes, relief, rivers and early high-status areas attract similar uses, which then expand outward along routes (Hoyt), e.g. industrial corridors along railways. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: 75.1 people per km²

items.stem: Suggest two reasons why many cities now have several centres rather than one CBD.
items.answer: Car ownership and ring roads allowed out-of-town retail and business parks; high CBD land costs and congestion pushed firms out; planning created new centres (e.g. La Défense, Paris).
items.markingKey: Car ownership and ring roads allowed out-of-town retail and business parks; high CBD land costs and congestion pushed firms out; planning created new centres (e.g. La Défense, Paris).

items.answer: They were based on 20th-century US cities; in many Latin American, African and Asian cities the poorest live on the periphery in informal settlements, colonial planning and rapid migration shape land use, and multiple centres develop.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Population data, Manchester city centre - 1991: about 1,000 residents; 2001: about 10,000; 2011: about 25,000; 2021: about 60,000.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase 2011-2021. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, identify the process shown and suggest two causes. [6]
items.answer: (a) (60,000 − 25,000)/25,000 × 100 = +140.0% (b) Reurbanisation: conversion of warehouses and new apartment towers; growth of service jobs and universities; regeneration after the 1996 IRA bombing.
items.markingKey: (a) (60,000 − 25,000)/25,000 × 100 = +140.0% (b) Reurbanisation: conversion of warehouses and new apartment towers; growth of service jobs and universities; regeneration after the 1996 IRA bombing. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: "Urban land-use models have little value in understanding contemporary cities." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Models remain useful as simplified frameworks but must be adapted to local contexts.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: based on early 20th-century US cities; ignore planning, culture and globalisation; Global South cities differ greatly. Arguments challenging it: bid-rent and accessibility principles still explain land values; models provide a framework for comparison. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Models remain useful as simplified frameworks but must be adapted to local contexts. Paper 2 Section C markbands [15]: 13-15 thorough response to all demands including the command term; accurate, detailed geographical knowledge and terminology; well-chosen, located and quantified examples at more than one scale; explicit, balanced evaluation (perspectives, places, scales, time) with a well-substantiated conclusion. 10-12 most demands addressed; accurate knowledge; examples relevant and developed; evaluation is balanced but not sustained. 7-9 some demands addressed; knowledge mostly accurate; examples partly developed; evaluation partial or one-sided. 4-6 limited, mainly descriptive; generalised examples; little evaluation. 1-3 little relevant knowledge; no examples or evaluation. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gentrification"?
options: The movement of higher-income residents into a lower-income area, upgrading housing and often displacing existing residents
The location of a settlement in relation to its surroundings, such as routes, resources and other settlements
Shopping centres and retail parks located on the edge of urban areas, close to major roads and with large car parks
The movement of people from large urban areas to smaller towns and rural areas beyond the city
items.answer: The movement of higher-income residents into a lower-income area, upgrading housing and often displacing existing residents
items.markingKey: A. "gentrification" is the movement of higher-income residents into a lower-income area, upgrading housing and often displacing existing residents.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "range"?
options: The maximum distance people are willing to travel to obtain a good or service
The ranking of settlements by size and the range of functions and services they provide
The most accessible point of the CBD with the highest land values
The physical characteristics of the land on which a settlement is built, e.g. a defensive hill, bridging point or water supply
items.answer: The maximum distance people are willing to travel to obtain a good or service
items.markingKey: A. "range" is the maximum distance people are willing to travel to obtain a good or service.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deindustrialisation"?
options: Economic activity that is not regulated, taxed or protected by the state, such as street vending, waste picking and small workshops
The decline of manufacturing employment and output in a region or country
The movement of higher-income residents into a lower-income area, upgrading housing and often displacing existing residents
Christaller's (1933) model explaining the size, number and spacing of settlements as market centres, using threshold and range
items.answer: The decline of manufacturing employment and output in a region or country
items.markingKey: B. "deindustrialisation" is the decline of manufacturing employment and output in a region or country.

items.stem: Explain the difference between counter-urbanisation and suburbanisation.
items.answer: Suburbanisation moves people to the edges of the same urban area; counter-urbanisation moves them beyond it to small towns and rural areas.
items.markingKey: Suburbanisation moves people to the edges of the same urban area; counter-urbanisation moves them beyond it to small towns and rural areas. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The largest settlement always provides the most specialised functions in a region." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Usually true, but some small settlements have specialised functions (resorts, university towns, administrative capitals).
items.markingKey: Usually true, but some small settlements have specialised functions (resorts, university towns, administrative capitals). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "The informal sector is the same as illegal activity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most informal work (vending, repairs, recycling) is legal but unregistered and unprotected.
items.markingKey: Most informal work (vending, repairs, recycling) is legal but unregistered and unprotected. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Counter-urbanisation means cities are declining in all high-income countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many cities grow through reurbanisation and immigration even as some residents leave for rural areas.
items.markingKey: Many cities grow through reurbanisation and immigration even as some residents leave for rural areas. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between situation and site.
items.answer: Site refers to the physical land a settlement is built on (e.g. a river terrace); situation refers to its location relative to surrounding features, routes and settlements (e.g. at a crossroads).
items.markingKey: Site refers to the physical land a settlement is built on (e.g. a river terrace); situation refers to its location relative to surrounding features, routes and settlements (e.g. at a crossroads). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the informal sector is large in cities of low-income countries.
items.answer: Rapid urban growth exceeds formal job creation; migrants lack skills or documents; the informal sector has easy entry and low capital needs; regulations and taxes are costly to comply with.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rapid urban growth exceeds formal job creation; migrants lack skills or documents; the informal sector has easy entry and low capital needs; regulations and taxes are costly to comply with. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tanzania has a total population of 123.1 million, of whom 72.5 million live in urban areas. Calculate the level of urbanisation.
items.markingKey: M1 urban ÷ total × 100; A1 58.9%.

items.stem: Using a named city, describe how its land use compares with one urban model.
items.answer: e.g. Rio de Janeiro fits the Griffin-Ford model in part: a CBD (Centro), an elite spine along the coast (Copacabana, Ipanema, Barra), and favelas both on hillsides near the centre (Rocinha) and on the periphery.
items.markingKey: e.g. Rio de Janeiro fits the Griffin-Ford model in part: a CBD (Centro), an elite spine along the coast (Copacabana, Ipanema, Barra), and favelas both on hillsides near the centre (Rocinha) and on the periphery.

items.stem: A data table shows the number of private cars registered in a Latin American capital: 1990 - 1,889,522 vehicles; 2010 - 3,407,939 vehicles. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (3,407,939 − 1,889,522) ÷ 1,889,522 × 100; A1 +80.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Using a named example, describe the process of reurbanisation and one consequence.
items.answer: e.g. Manchester: city-centre population grew from about 1,000 (1990s) to over 60,000 by the 2020s through apartment building in former warehouses and new towers; consequence - rising rents and gentrification of nearby Ancoats.
items.markingKey: e.g. Manchester: city-centre population grew from about 1,000 (1990s) to over 60,000 by the 2020s through apartment building in former warehouses and new towers; consequence - rising rents and gentrification of nearby Ancoats.

items.stem: With reference to Chicago in the 1920s, explain how it illustrates the concentric zone model.
items.answer: Burgess observed rings of land use from the Loop (CBD) outwards. Immigrants arriving in the zone in transition and wealthier groups moving outward produced a ring pattern.
items.markingKey: Context (Burgess observed rings of land use from the Loop (CBD) outwards.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Immigrants arriving in the zone in transition and wealthier groups moving outward produced a ring pattern. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the concentric zone model.

items.stem: Using a named city, outline two consequences of deindustrialisation.
items.answer: e.g. Detroit: population fell by about two-thirds, leaving tens of thousands of vacant homes; the city declared bankruptcy in 2013 with about US$18 billion of debt.
items.markingKey: e.g. Detroit: population fell by about two-thirds, leaving tens of thousands of vacant homes; the city declared bankruptcy in 2013 with about US$18 billion of debt.

items.stem: Between 1990 and 2010 the urban population of a South Asian state changed from 23.0 to 24.3 million. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (24.3 − 23.0) ÷ 23.0 × 100; A1 +5.7% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Settlement survey description: a region has 1 city (population 450,000, 120 services), 4 towns (about 30,000, 35 services), 16 villages (about 2,000, 6 services) and 60 hamlets (under 200, 0-1 services).

(a) Describe the urban hierarchy shown. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain the relationship using threshold and range. [6]
items.answer: (a) A pyramid-shaped hierarchy: few large settlements with many services and many small settlements with few services. (b) Large populations exceed the thresholds of high-order services, so these are only found in the city; small settlements support only low-order services with small thresholds.
items.markingKey: (a) A pyramid-shaped hierarchy: few large settlements with many services and many small settlements with few services. (b) Large populations exceed the thresholds of high-order services, so these are only found in the city; small settlements support only low-order services with small thresholds. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: Examine the view that deindustrialised cities can successfully reinvent their economies.
items.answer: Reinvention is possible with investment and strategy, but benefits are unevenly shared.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: Manchester and the Ruhr developed services, culture and education; regeneration attracts investment and residents. Against / limitations: Detroit and other Rust Belt cities still face poverty; new jobs may not suit former industrial workers. A supported conclusion might be: Reinvention is possible with investment and strategy, but benefits are unevenly shared. Paper 1 extended-response markbands [10]: 9-10 responds to all demands of the question; accurate, detailed knowledge and understanding; well-developed, relevant examples and case studies with specific (named, located, quantified) detail; balanced, well-structured evaluation leading to a substantiated conclusion. 7-8 responds to most demands; mostly accurate knowledge; examples relevant but not always fully developed; evaluation present but uneven. 5-6 some demands addressed; knowledge partly accurate; examples general or loosely linked; evaluation mostly implicit. 3-4 limited, largely descriptive; little use of examples. 1-2 little relevant knowledge or understanding. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: "Urbanisation brings more benefits than costs to low-income countries." Discuss this statement, with reference to examples you have studied.
items.answer: Urbanisation is central to development; costs depend on how well it is planned and governed.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: higher incomes, services and productivity; cities generate most GDP; lower fertility and better access to education. Against / limitations: slums, congestion and pollution (Lagos, Dhaka); informal work and inequality. A supported conclusion might be: Urbanisation is central to development; costs depend on how well it is planned and governed. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that physical site factors are no longer important in explaining the growth of cities.
items.answer: Situation and human factors dominate growth today, but site still shapes city form and risk.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: global connections, policy and investment drive growth (Dubai, Shenzhen); technology overcomes site limits (reclamation, desalination). Against / limitations: coasts, rivers and harbours still shape the largest cities; site affects hazards and expansion (Hong Kong, Mexico City). A supported conclusion might be: Situation and human factors dominate growth today, but site still shapes city form and risk.
